..
Issued at 329 AM CDT Wed Aug 12 2026

Forecast remains complex within our persistent pattern of active
weather. Main concern in the near term is the potential for
another fast-moving line of wind-producing storms across at
least a portion of the area later this morning/midday. 

A nearly stationary frontal boundary remains in place across 
the Midwest early this morning, stretching roughly from near 
Omaha to north of Des Moines to Milwaukee. Complicating the 
surface pattern however, is the remnant outflow boundary from 
Tuesday's derecho, which intersects the front near Waterloo, IA 
and extends southeast and bisects IL along a SQI-BMI-MTO-EVV 
line. The west/northwest periphery of the cold pool appears to 
be fairly shallow however, per 00Z DVN and ILX soundings (as 
compared to ILM farther to the east/southeast). Aloft, a subtle
mid-level short wave has been evident in GOES vapor imagery 
transiting northern IA and entering northwest IL, inducing a 
modest west-southwest 25-30 kt low level jet from northern MO 
into northern/central IL/IN. With an axis of 3500-4000 J/kg 
MUCAPE along/north of the front/outflow boundary across the 
region, there's been concern since last evening for the 
potential to develop elevated convection within a northwest- 
southeast arc across the area (along/northeast of the remnant 
outflow boundary). So far however, only isolated updraft 
attempts have been noted and successive CAM runs have backed off
considerably in convective coverage across the forecast area 
through daybreak. That said, we'll have to continue to monitor 
for any deeper updraft development, as the environment would 
support the potential for strong elevated storms with a hail 
threat if they develop.

Of greater concern this morning, is an MCS which has been 
developing southeast from western South Dakota into northern 
Nebraska overnight in association with an attendant mid-level 
short wave and MCV. There is notable CAM support indicating this
MCS becoming more organized across eastern NE/western IA toward
daybreak, then propagating quickly eastward along the 
aforementioned surface front/outflow boundaries into our IL cwa 
after 14/15Z (9-10 AM) this morning. While not quite as robust 
as yesterday's derecho, high-res guidance does explicitly 
indicate 60-70 mph winds across parts of our forecast area with 
this MCS. CAMs indicate an easterly propagation of this system 
across the cwa, though with the remnant outflow likely mixing 
back north across the southern half of our cwa that may support 
more of an east-southeast or southeast track as we saw 
yesterday. SPC has pulled their new Day 1 slight (level 2 of 5) 
severe risk up to about a Dixon-Renssalear line. It's possible 
that could be adjusted further if the evolution of the MCS 
supports it later this morning. For now, will be advertising the
severe threat (primarily wind) even a little north of that for 
this morning/midday. Thunderstorm threat should then diminish 
markedly from the west into this afternoon in the wake of the 
MCS and parent short wave.

There may be somewhat of a lull in convection 
coverage/potential tonight into early Thursday morning, 
depending on the footprint of the anticipated MCS cold pool, and
with some weak mid-level height rises indicated in model 
guidance. Have trimmed pops during this period especially up 
north along the IL/WI border and Lake Michigan. Another mid-
level wave (currently over NV/UT) is then progged move into the 
region on Thursday which look to increase shower and 
thunderstorm chances again during the day and with additional 
rounds through at least Thursday night. These continued rounds 
of storms will maintain at least a marginal severe threat and 
a threat of flash flooding if storms train over the same areas.

Unfortunately, medium-range guidance continues to depict our 
active pattern remaining in place across the region into the 
weekend. There does appear to be decent agreement in the global 
models/ensembles that high pressure eventually settles across 
the western Lakes region by Monday-Tuesday of next week, pushing
our stalled frontal zone to the south and providing a period of
dry weather at that time.

Ratzer
